Applied AI & Data  ·  AI Control Can you stop it? Have you tried?

Every claim about a system being under control resolves to three things: a written limit, a record that someone reads, and a stop that has actually been pulled. We build all three, and we pull the stop before it matters.

6–10 WEEKSCONTROLS BUILT AND EXERCISEDEVIDENCE AN AUDITOR ACCEPTS
The decisions underneath

Three questions decide the design.

Control is not a document. It is a set of things that either happen at the moment they are needed, or do not.

01

Who set the limit, and when

A limit set once, by a person who has since left, against a business that has since doubled, is a historical artifact rather than a control.

02

Does anybody read the log

A record nobody reads exists for the audit. That is useful, but it should not be counted as a control.

03

Has the stop ever been pulled

An untested kill switch is a claim. We exercise it on the running system, in daylight, and write down how long it took.

The boundary

We build and exercise the controls. Someone independent attests to them.

Three steps. We build the limits, logs and stops and pull them on the running system. An independent party gives the opinion, and we fix what it finds.

STEP 01 · ORVIX

We build and exercise

We build the limits, the logs and the stop. Then we trip each limit, read the log it produced and pull the stop, timing the whole thing.

STEP 02 · INDEPENDENT REVIEWER

An independent party attests

The opinion on whether the controls operate comes from outside the team that built them, using the exercise results we record.

STEP 03 · ORVIX

We re-exercise on a cycle

Controls are exercised again on a schedule, because a control that worked once worked against a configuration that has since changed.

Every stop we build is pulled before the system carries anything that matters.

Questions we are asked

Before you ask us.

Is this the same as AI governance?
They meet, but they are different work. Governance decides what should be true and records the decision; AI Control builds the mechanism that makes it true and produces the evidence that it operated. Governance without control is intention; control without governance is unexplained machinery.
We already have a policy and an approval workflow.
Then the useful question is approval latency, meaning how long each approval takes. If approvals are granted in seconds at volume, the control has been abandoned in practice while it still exists on paper. That is a finding worth having before anyone else makes it.
Do you take over running the controls?
We build them and hand them over with a named owner. If you want them operated, our AI Cybersecurity team can run them, and the assurance opinion on anything we operate still comes from an independent party.
What if a system has no controls at all?
That is common, and it is not a moral failure. It is what happens when a capability arrives faster than the governance calendar. The first useful output is usually a complete list.

When did you last pull the stop?

Name the system you would find hardest to halt on a Friday afternoon. In thirty minutes we will work out what stopping it would take.
